intervention.description: in situ STEM heating and molecular dynamics simulations to investigate thermal behavior

structure.description: strong structural and chemical evolutions with formation of an AuCu layer at the surface

evidence_units.mechanism: pronounced atomic diffusion that is surprisingly more active in these quinary nanoalloys than in monometallic and bimetallic subsystems

outcome.property: formation and melting of AuCu layer
outcome.measurement_method: in situ aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and molecular dynamics simulations

comparison.direction: atomic diffusion is more active in quinary nanoalloys

evidence_spans: Here, in situ aberration‐corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and molecular dynamics simulations are combined to investigate at the atomic scale the thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles (NPs) from 298 to 973 K.

Both in situ STEM heating and atomistic simulations reveal strong structural and chemical evolutions in the NPs with the formation and melting of an AuCu layer at the surface of NPs at high temperature.

This phase separation that appears progressively with temperature is driven by pronounced atomic diffusion that is surprisingly more active in these quinary nanoalloys than in monometallic and bimetallic subsystems.
limitations: ruling out the existence of sluggish diffusion
lowering their temperature range of application

evidence_spans: In the present work, we used in situ scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), corroborated with atomistic simulations, to study in real‐time and at the atomic scale the structural and compositional evolution of AuCoCuNiPt NPs from 298 to 973 K.
These in situ insights into the thermodynamic properties of AuCoCuNiPt HENA reveal their poor structural stability at high temperature due to atomic diffusion that cannot be considered as sluggish.
limitations: experimental evidence of sluggish diffusion in HENA is lacking

material.name: AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles
material.initial_state: as-prepared, monocrystalline or multi-twinned FCC, diameter 3-6.5 nm, uniform composition

intervention.description: In situ heating TEM on a heating microchip to observe structural and compositional evolution

outcome.value: size distribution widens to 13 nm; shape ratio increases (elliptical to spherical); NP density decreases sharply
outcome.measurement_method: STEM HAADF images and size distribution analysis

comparison.baseline_state: uniform composition, 3-6.5 nm diameter, monocrystalline or multi-twinned

intervention.description: Heating to 773-873 K to induce coalescence and phase separation

structure.description: Coalescence events occur in several minutes; high-contrast areas appear at the surface of just merged NPs indicating phase separation

evidence_units.mechanism: Atomic diffusion within nanostructures at 773 and 873 K tends to segregate Au and Cu at the surface; segregation is observed only in coalesced nanostructures where atom mobility is more important

outcome.value: high-contrast areas exclusively made of Au-Cu
outcome.measurement_method: STEM HAADF imaging and STEM-EDS mapping

comparison.baseline_state: homogenous distribution of all metals (5 nm NPs that did not coalesce)

evidence_spans: Evidently, coalescence phenomena speed up as the temperature rises. At 773 and 873 K coalescence and reshaping occur in several minutes ( Figure 3 a,b ) while at 973 K it lasts only a few seconds (Figure 3c ). Interestingly, phase separation is frequently observed during the coalescence of two sup‐5 nm NPs at 773 and 873 K. As illustrated in the STEM HAADF images in Figure 3a,b , high‐contrast areas appear at the surface of just merged NPs. These heterogenous contrasts evidence the segregation of metals with different atomic numbers during coalescence events and they are still observed after the subsequent reshaping of the coalesced nanostructures (Figure S3 , Supporting Information). Moreover, STEM‐EDS mapping performed at the single NP scale revealed that 5 nm NPs that did not coalesce maintained a well‐homogenous distribution of all metals ( Figure 4 a ), but the high‐contrast areas observed in larger coalesced NPs are exclusively made of Au‐Cu (Figure 4b ). These results suggest that atomic diffusion within the nanostructures at 773 and 873 K tends to segregate Au and Cu at the surface but the resulting Janus configuration can be only observed in coalesced nanostructures in which atom mobility is more important.

intervention.description: Raising temperature to 973 K to drive active atomic diffusion and phase separation

structure.description: All NPs reduce in size; complete loss of gold and copper; resulting distribution of Co, Ni, and Pt remains homogeneous; NPs remain crystalline with FCC structure

evidence_units.mechanism: Atomic diffusion is active enough to drive phase separation; segregation of Au and Cu at the NP surface followed by melting and evaporation of the Au-Cu shell due to lowest melting temperatures of these two metals

outcome.value: size reduction of 22% in first minutes; complete loss of Au and Cu
outcome.measurement_method: STEM HAADF images and STEM-EDX nano-analysis

evidence_spans: At 973 K, atomic diffusion is active enough to drive a phase separation in all nanostructures. Indeed, just after raising the temperature from 873 to 973 K, all the NPs reduce in size. As this phenomenon overlaps with the coalescence that is very active at 973 K, this size decrease is not captured in the size distribution measured after 15 min at 973 K (Figure 2b ). However as shown in Figure 3d,e , we measure a size reduction of 22% of all the observed NPs within the first minutes at 973 K. Accordingly, a complete loss of gold and copper is evidenced by STEM‐EDS, while at lower temperatures the composition of NPs was quite stable (Figure 3f and Figure S4 , Supporting Information). The loss of Au and Cu from the NPs at 973 K is most likely due to the segregation of these two metals at the NP surface followed by the melting and evaporation of the Au‐Cu shell. It is worth noting that Au and Cu have the lowest melting temperature of the five metals (Table S1 , Supporting Information) and the melting of Au, Cu, and AuCu NPs was also observed by TEM at 973 K in previous reports. material.name: AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticle
material.initial_state: solid solution with random distribution, perfect crystalline NP

intervention.description: Investigating thermal properties at different temperatures to observe segregation

structure.description: At low temperatures (500 K), solid solution; as temperature increases, gold- and copper-enriched zones appear at the surface; loss of faceting where Au and Cu segregate; at 1000 K, surface layer consists essentially of gold and copper; at 1100 K, transition from solid to liquid state observed

evidence_units.mechanism: Segregation driving forces include cohesion (surface energy difference), size (atomic radii difference), and alloying; surface energy is a major driving force where bulk atoms have much lower energy than surface atoms, favoring stabilization of Co, Ni, Pt in the core and presence of Au, Cu at the surface

outcome.value: Au concentration increases up to ≈900 K; at ≈1000 K, Ni and Co drop below 0.1%, Pt close to zero, surface layer essentially Au and Cu
outcome.direction: increase for Au/Cu, decrease for Ni/Co/Pt

evidence_spans: At low temperatures (500 K), a solid solution is clearly identified: the atoms are distributed in a fully random distribution within a perfectly crystalline NP displaying (111) facets. As the temperature increases, gold‐ and copper‐enriched zones appear at the surface of the NP. The cross‐sectional view further reveals that the presence of these elements alters the local surface structure with a loss of faceting where Au and Cu segregate. In contrast, surface areas where this segregation is not observed have preserved their faceted aspect. Between 1000 and 1200 K, the proportion of copper and gold at the surface becomes predominant and the complete transition from solid to liquid state is observed, as confirmed by the pair correlation function analysis presented in Figure S10 (Supporting Information). To quantify these segregation effects, Figure 5b displays the surface concentration for each element at different temperatures. Below 500 K, we notice that the surface exhibits a structure made of all the elements with a slightly lower proportion of platinum. Then, a change of slope is noticed with an increase in Au at the expense of Pt up to ≈900 K. Last, ≈1000 K the concentration of nickel and cobalt atoms drops drastically (below 0.1%), while that of platinum is close to zero giving rise to a surface layer consisting essentially of gold and copper.

material.name: CoNiCuPtAu nanoparticles
material.form: two icosahedral NPs close to each other

intervention.description: Simulating coalescence of two NPs to study diffusion and segregation effects

structure.description: Coalescence occurs after a few ps; formation of a NP whose surface is highly enriched in copper and gold atoms; Au segregation is more important in the coalesced structure than for a single icosahedron

evidence_units.mechanism: Reshaping of nanostructures boosts atomic diffusion; neck region presents strong interdiffusion activity to increase radius of neck and reduce surface curvature; higher self-diffusivity of Au in neck region leads to stronger segregation

outcome.property: self-diffusivity of Au and surface concentration
outcome.value: higher D self in neck region; more pronounced Au segregation in coalesced structure
outcome.measurement_method: Einstein relation calculation in MD simulation

evidence_spans: As seen in Figure 6 a–f , coalescence occurs, after a few ps, with the formation of a NP whose surface is again highly enriched in copper and gold atoms. Interestingly, the Au segregation is more important in the case of the structure resulting from coalescence than for the single icosahedron. This is clearly visible in Figure 6g , where the gold concentration at the surface is presented in both situations, showing a more pronounced segregation in the structure after coalescence. Note that only the diffusion of individual atoms is considered here whereas coalescence can involve collective motions of atoms as highlighted in reference. [ [14] ] However, the main conclusions of the present study about neck‐enhanced segregation mechanisms are not expected to be altered. To better decipher the segregation mechanisms, we investigate the impact of coalescence on the diffusion of gold atoms within the nanostructures. To this end, the self‐diffusivity (D self ) of Au was calculated using the Einstein relation (Note S1 , Supporting Information) in different areas of the coalesced nanostructure. As the temperature rises, a linear increase in the self‐diffusivity of Au atoms is observed until a change in the slope corresponds to the phase transition from solid to liquid (Figure 6h ). Furthermore, a higher D self is revealed in the neck region close to the interface between the two NPs. This neck region is known to present a strong interdiffusion activity in order to increase the radius of the neck and reduce its surface curvature. [ [15] ] Therefore, the stronger segregation of Au and Cu observed both experimentally and theoretically in coalesced HENA is most likely due to the reshaping of the nanostructures that boost atomic diffusion.

intervention.description: alternating deposition of pure metals using a COMPex KrF excimer laser in a high vacuum chamber

structure.description: FCC multi-twin nanostructures with many NPs presenting an icosahedral shape

outcome.measurement_method: in situ TEM and STEM imaging

evidence_spans: Pulsed laser deposition has been widely used for the synthesis of bimetallic nanoalloys. [ [17] , [18] ] The fabrication method permits an alternating deposition of pure metals on the substrate to form nanoalloys of controlled size and composition, using a COMPex KrF excimer laser beam in a high vacuum chamber.
In the present study, the same HENA was directly synthetized on the SiN membrane of a heating MEMS chip commercialized by Protochips for in situ TEM investigations.
A substrate temperature of 873 K, a laser frequency of 5 Hz, and a total nominal thickness of 4 nm measured prior to metal deposition were measured with a quartz crystal microbalance.
As seen experimentally, HENA prepared by PLD are FCC multi‐twinned nanostructures and many NPs present an icosahedral shape.

material.name: HENA (AuCoCuNiPt)
material.composition: equiatomic (for simulation) / sub-10 nm near equiatomic (experiment)

intervention.description: heating of NPs on SiN membrane in a gas-cell TEM setup to monitor evolution

structure.description: Evolution of HENA structure at high temperatures

evidence_units.mechanism: HENA continuously evolves at high temperatures; analysis time limited to prevent further evolution during measurement; cooling to room temperature required for accurate EDS analysis due to IR radiation effects.
evidence_spans: As HENA continuously evolves at high temperatures, the analysis time at each temperature was limited to 45 min.

We had to go back to 298 K after each temperature step to perform EDS analyses to avoid the adverse effect on the X‐ray detection efficiency of IR radiation emitted from the heating device at high temperatures.
limitations: Analysis time at each temperature limited to 45 min due to continuous evolution
Required return to 298 K for EDS analysis to avoid IR radiation interference

material.name: Cu-Au-Co-Ni-Pt NPs
material.initial_state: relaxed at 0.01 K using conjugated gradient method

intervention.description: simulating NPs with EAM potential (Zhou et al.) and Nose-Hoover thermostat

parameters.monitoring_criteria: plateau of total energy and surface concentration

evidence_units.mechanism: Defects (icosahedral structure) influence atomic diffusion and metal segregation; simulations monitor surface concentration and total energy to determine equilibrium.

outcome.measurement_method: averages of last 50 ns of simulations

evidence_spans: Molecular Dynamic (MD) simulations are performed using the open source Large‐scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulators (LAMMPS) package. [ [21] ] In order to investigate Cu‐Au‐Co‐Ni‐Pt NPs, the Embedded Atom Method (EAM) potential derived by Zhou et al. is used to describe the interaction between different atomic pairs.

As defects can influence atomic diffusion and metal segregation, [ [24] ] we investigate NPs in an icosahedral structure having a five‐fold symmetry and containing 309, 923, 2057, and 3871 randomly distributed on the FCC multi‐twinned lattice.

Regarding the MD simulations at a given temperature, the evolution of both the total energy and the surface concentration of each element is monitored and considered complete when these two quantities reach a plateau (Figure S9 , Supporting Information).

Finally, all the quantities analyzed (surface concentration, atomic energy, diffusion, etc.) are derived from the averages of a set of configurations (corresponding to approximately the last 50 ns of simulations) where the plateau is reached.
Knowing that thermodynamic equilibrium is difficult to achieve at low temperature, complementary simulations were reproduced at lower heating rate (1K ns −1 ).
limitations: Thermodynamic equilibrium difficult to achieve at low temperature; complementary simulations at lower heating rate (1K ns⁻¹) performed

intervention.description: comparing gold segregation between icosahedron and truncated octahedron of the same size

evidence_units.mechanism: Shape of NPs influences their thermal stability and segregation behavior.
evidence_spans: From a theoretical point of view, we made the choice to study icosahedral NPs that are similar to those observed experimentally but beyond size effects, [ [25] ] the shape of NPs can also have an influence on their thermal stability. [ [26] ] This last point is illustrated in Figure S17 (Supporting Information) where the gold segregation in case of an icosahedron and truncated octahedron of the same size is presented.
